# Results

The progression of model development from the 2023 diagnostic model to the 2026 diagnostic model is described in Section @sec-stepwise and the results are displayed in Figure @fig-stepwise-panel and Figure @fig-stepwise-panel-reduce. The stepwise analysis changes are discussed briefly below, each step compared to the previous step. The stepwise development should only be considered indicative of changes, because the models in each step do not undergo thorough diagnostics and tuning. The diagnostic model represents the culmination of a numbers steps that incorporate changes from the previous assessment, many of which have been suggested and/or recommended through peer discussion at the Pre-assessment Workshop (PAW) or in response to comments from the SC on the previous assessment. Others relate to new data or biological information and changes the analysts decide were useful and could improve the model from their experimentation. The diagnostic model may or may not be the best possible model for the data, in fact it rarely if ever will be with the limited time to follow the many avenues of possible improvement. The diagnostic model is also not a model for management advice. It should be viewed as an experimental model for exploring model behaviour and performance, and it should pass the common performance diagnostics to provide a basis model for sensitivity analyses to inform the structure and components of the model grid or ensemble that is used to construct management advice.

1.  **\[01\]** 2023 diagnostic-model refit: no change in $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ or $SB$.

2.  **\[02\]** New MFCL executable, and ini update (1007): very minor changes in early recruitment, no other changes $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ or $SB$.

3.  **\[03\]** Lorenzen natural-mortality scaling fixed to the 2023 diagnostic-model estimate: very minor changes in $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ and $SB$.

4.  **\[04\]** Minor update to length-weight conversion factors: very minor changes in $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ and $SB$.

5.  **\[05\]** Convert to the 5 region structure, and new fishery definitions 33-fishery structure (28 extraction, 5 index): reductions in historical levels pre-1990s, but very minor changes in terminal $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ and $SB$.

6.  **\[06\]** Size-composition inputs replaced with the reweighted weight data converted to lengths for longline fisheries, data until 2021: very minor change in $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ and $SB$.

7.  **\[07\]** Weight-as-length plus more recent observed-length compositions for longline fisheries, data until 2021: very minor change $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ and $SB$

8.  **\[08\]** Update all data sets to 2024, except CAAL: **first notable change**, some increase (less depleted) in $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ and $SB$, particularly since mid 1990s.

9.  **\[09\]** Apply the size data truncations to the ID and PH fisheries size data as per previous assessments: no change in $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ and $SB$.

10. **\[10\]** Switch to separate sdmTMB regional CPUE indices and apply the MFCL regional scaling penalty feature based on a global sdmTMB model, time period 1965-1969 (max spatial coverage): **second notable change**, shift to lower (more depleted) $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ and $SB$.

11. **\[11\]** Time-varying CPUE uncertainty: very minor change in $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ or $SB$.

12. **\[12\]** Fixed regional CPUE SDs: very minor change in $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ or $SB$.

13. **\[13\]** Update CAAL data, raw unweighted data update: **third clear but not major change**, reduction (more depleted ) in $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ and $SB$.

14. **\[14a\]** Reweighted CAAL data based on the model region global CPUE sdmTMB relative mean density: **fourth clear but not major change**, reversed the previous step with an increase (less depleted) in $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ and $SB$.

15. **\[14b\]** Reweighted CAAL data based on the model region global CPUE sdmTMB relative mean density, but with region 3 and 4 merged: minor reduction in (more depleted) $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ and $SB$.

16. **\[15\]** Selectivity modifications, flexible fishery-specific selectivity plus weak F10 non-decreasing penalty

17. **\[16\]** Implement release group specific period mixing periods, K-statistic cut-off 0.2: **fifth clear but not major change** reduction (more depleted) $SB_{F=0}$, $SB$ and $SB$.

18. **\[17\]** Deactivate the reporting rate adjustments during mixing: **sixth and most notable scaling impact**, substantial increase in historical and terminal (less depleted) $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ and $SB$.

19. **\[18** Add effort creep adjustment to the regional CPUE abundance indices: increase in terminal (less depleted) $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ and $SB$, higher early $SB$ and $SB_{F=0}$ with steeper decline $SB$.

20. **\[19\]** Implement Dirichlet multinomial on size data, maximum effective sample size 25: minor decrease (more depleted) in $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ and $SB$.

21. **\[20\]** Tau ($\tau$)=2: **seventh and largest scaling impact**, caused a reduction (more depleted) $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ just below 0.2, and an approximate halving of the population scale $SB$.

22. **\[21\]** Add weak non-decreasing penalty on F33 (region 5 index): minor change to $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ and $SB$.

23. **\[22\]** Steepness increased from 0.8 - 0.9, more defensible steepness for a tropical tuna, consistent with mode of ensemble distribution: minor change to $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ and $SB$.

24. **Diagnostic2026**

The stepwise model development can be explored in the [interactive HTML viewer](https://pacificcommunity.github.io/ofp-sam-bet-2026-stepwise/interactive-model-viewer.html).

Overall, only minor to moderate changes in the stepwise (terminal estimates, compared to prior step) were observed when updating the data to 2024 (less depleted/higher spawning potential), implementing the new CPUE approach (more depleted/lower spawning potential), implementing the release group specific mixing period (moderately more depleted/minor lowering in spawning potential), effort creep (perhaps counter intuitive, slightly less depleted/higher spawning potential), and implementing Dirichlet multinomial (slightly more depleted/slightly lower spawning potential). The increased initial biomass, steeper decline and slightly higher terminal biomass and less depleted stock status after implementation of the effort creep was perhaps counter intuitive. However, each effort creep scenario is a separate set of CPUE indices that the model fits to, so the starting biomass can shift. An alternative approach to a better understand effort creep impacts would be to some how fix the starting biomass conditions to be the same across the different effort creep adjusted CPUE time series. We necessarily treat the alternative effort creep CPUE scenarios as independent hypotheses and run new model fits to each, but this is an area that needs more thought.

The most notable changes in the stepwise were related to tag data, initially, (step 17) deactivating the application of reporting rate adjustments in the mixing period. This change was as expected and noted earlier, higher spawning potential and less depleted status if reporting rate adjustments are not made. This confirms the importance of this decision on the influence of tag data on population scaling, and it being included in the uncertainty ensemble. It should be noted that while the direction of this effect will likely be consistent across mixing period assumptions, the degree of impact will be variable depending on the mixing period applied to the individual release groups and observed tag recaptures. We also suggest both options for dealing with reporting rates in the mixing period are not ideal, and this issue requires further consideration. By far the biggest stepwise result was from increasing the fixed value of $\tau$ from 1 (Poisson) to 2 (negative binomial) (step 20) Figure @fig-stepwise-panel-reduce. This resulted in the population scaling approximately halving and the terminal depletion dropping to $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ just below 0.2. This major shift reflected the downweighting of the tag data in the joint likelihood, and signals that in the current assessment the tagging data has a strong influence on increasing the biomass scale and reducing the stock depletion (more optimistic stock status). This is discussed further below in relation to the likelihood profiles and sensitivity analysis results.

Fit of the diagnostic model to data sources {#sec-fit-diag}
-------------------------------------------

### Standardized CPUE: index fisheries {#sec-fit-cpue}

The model fits to the index fishery standardised CPUE data were generally quite good for the main trends and dynamics for all model regions (Figure @fig-cpue-fit-1-5). Exceptions were the later period in model region 1 were the fit deteriorated in later 15 years, and the model tended to predict higher CPUE than the majority of the observations. Similarly, the model over predicted the early period observation in region 3, but tended to underpredict the later period observations (Figure @fig-cpue-resids-1-5)

### Size composition data {#fit_sizecomp}

Here we focus on aggregated fits to the length composition data.

**Longline fisheries:** The aggregate model fits to the length composition data for the longline extraction (fisheries 1-11) and longline index fisheries (fisheries 29-33), (Figure @fig-length-fit-aggregated-ll), were good for all the extraction and index fisheries, with the exception of the region 5 index fishery, that has very poor size data coverage, and the model overestimated the frequencies of larger size frequencies, and underestimated small to medium size frequencies. The LL.ALL extraction fishery in region 5 has slightly more data and a better fit.

The time series plots of observed versus predicted mean lengths for the longline fisheries were acceptable for most fisheries, particularly for those fisheries with consistent data coverage and narrower confidence intervals across time (Figure @fig-length-fit-timeseries-ll). The index fisheries were acceptable, although for region 1 the model struggled to predict the observed extent of the decline in mean length, although still estimating a long-term decline.

**Other fisheries:** The aggregated length composition fits were also quite good for most of the non-longline fisheries (Figure @fig-length-fit-aggregated-dompl) and purse seine fisheries (Figure @fig-length-fit-aggregated-ps). The time series plots of observed versus predicted mean lengths for the other fisheries were clearly better for the fisheries with more observed data, such as the Philippines purse seine fishery in region 2 and the important associated purse seine fishery in regions 3 that accounts for a large amount of the bigeye catch. The model predicted the mean length dynamics of this fishery quite well (Figure @fig-length-fit-timeseries-other.

### Tagging data {#sec-fit-tagging}

The model estimates of the aggregated tag attrition fit the observed tagging data relatively well (Figure @fig-tag-attrition-all), albeit with some overestimation of the number of tag returns between 10-15 quarters at liberty. We note that the tag attrition predictions were closer to the observations with tau of 1 (figure not included), possibly due to the higher weighting to fitting the tag data in that model.

For the tag recapture groups (Figure @fig-tag-recapture-fit-years-groups, there is notable variation in the numbers of recaptures across groups and time. Eight of the 16 groups dominate the recaptures. Recaptures estimated by the diagnostic model are well matched to the observations for dominant groups.

### Tag reporting rates {#sec-tag-reporting-rates}

The estimated tag reporting rates by fishery recapture groups (see groupings in Table @tbl-fisheries-definitions) are shown for RTTP and PTTP in Figure @fig-tag-report-rates-rttp-pttp and JTPT inFigure @fig-tag-report-rates-jtpt . As expected, the reporting rate estimates differ among fisheries groups and across tagging programs. For the RTTP and PTTP the reporting rate estimates for those groupings that received higher penalties (based on external estimated reporting rates from tag seeding i.e. 10, 7, 14, 17 and 18) were closer to the prior mean, for example groups 10, 7, 14 but groups 17 and 18 wanted higher reporting rates. One reporting rate group was stuck on the upper bound of 0.99. For the JPTP, where there are no informed reporting rate penalties, one group preferred higher reporting rates (group 19), two preferred lower (group 20 and 29) and one was on the upper bound (group 23).

### Conditional age-at-length {#sec-fit-CAAL}

The estimated growth curve for the diagnostic model, which is based on both the CAAL data and the size data is shown in Figure @fig-growth-curve. Aggregate fits to the conditional-age-at-length (CAAL) data are shown in Figure @fig-caal-fits. For length bins from around 70 to 120 cm, which constitute most of the observed CAAL data, the model's predicted median ages at lengths fit the observed data very well. At smaller sizes the model tends to slightly over predict the observed median age, for size bins from around 120 to 150 cm the model under predicts the median age, and for the largest sizes, the model prediction is closer to the observed median age at length. Overall the fit is reasonable.

At the model region level, region 1 has a reasonable amount of data, with the addition of the new samples form north of $10^{\circ}\,\mathrm{N}$) and shows the best fit, with the model estimates tracking the observed median ages at length well. Region 2 and region 4 have very low observed data, and the fit is poor for region 2, but reasonable for region 4. Region 3 and 5 have more data, and similar to the aggregated data, predict the observed data reasonably well up until around 120 cm, after with the median age at length tends to be under predicted.

Diagnostic analysis for the diagnostic model {#sec-diagnostics}
--------------------------------------------

### Convergence {#sec-diag-convergence}

The diagnostic model reach a gradient of 0.0001, and a positive definite Hessian (PDH) was achieved. Parameters on bound - add Parameter correlation - add

### Jitter {#sec-diag-jitter}

The jitter method conducted in the current assessment was more rigorous than the 2023 assessment with jittering from the early model fitting phases. Twenty-five of 30 runs met the convergence criterion. The lowest objective function value among retained runs was 89,469.7, 1,345.2 units lower than the Diagnostic model without jitter; 15 of the retained fits had worse fits and ten retained runs improved on that fit Figure @fig-jitter-scatter-plot. The minimum gradient was 5.84 × $10^{-4}$. The worse objective functions typically had much higher differences in the objective function value to the diagnostic model than the better values. This indicates some instability in the model convergence and the occurrence of local topography on the likelihood surface. However, the estimated management quantities showed minor variation among all jitter models. The estimated quantity that varied most among the jitter models was the recruitment, which seems to have unstable estimation Figure @fig-jitter-derived-values-diag-panel. For the depletion at the region level the estimation of the depletion in region 5 was most unstable Figure @fig-jitter-regional-depletion.

The complete jitter results can be viewed in the [browser report](https://pacificcommunity.github.io/ofp-sam-bet-2026-jitter/jitter-report.html).

### Self test {#sec-selftest}

Fifty of 50 pseudo-data refits completed and met the recorded convergence criterion. Convergence ranged from 5.13e-05 to 9.97e-05. Median whole-series pseudo-data errors ranged from -0.23% to 0.07%. The generating truth was inside the pointwise central 95% empirical refit range at 385 of 438 annual quantity-year points (87.9%). Median relative bias across recent and native assessment summaries ranged from -2.1% to 3.5%. Across the selected recruitment-scale, growth and stock-recruit parameters, median relative errors ranged from -3.85% to 2.00%. These are empirical simulation-estimation diagnostics under the configured generator, not confidence intervals for the assessment. Self test was overall successful, the model successful estimated the time series $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$, $SB$, recruitment without any consistent bias through the time series. Median relative bias was less than 5% for $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$, $SB$, recruitment and around 6-7% for F, which had a positive bias (Figure @fig-selftest-recovery). The selftest recovered time series of derived quantities is displayed in Figure @fig-selftest-time-series.

The complete self-test results can be viewed in the [browser report](https://pacificcommunity.github.io/ofp-sam-bet-2026-selftest/selftest-report.html).

### Retrospectives {#sec-retro-analysis}

The retrospective analysis showed acceptable results with no strong bias for depletion (Mohn's rho -0.195), recruitment (Mohn's rho -0.062) and spawning potential (Mohn's $\rho$ -0.235) all within or close to the acceptable range of $\pm 0.2 \text{ to } \pm 0.3$, fishing mortality had Mohn's $\rho$ of 0.308, but this is not unexpected as F is very uncertain in the final years of the assessment (Figure @fig-retro-analysis).

The complete retrospective results can be viewed in the [browser report](https://pacificcommunity.github.io/ofp-sam-bet-2026-retrospective/retrospective-report.html).

### Likelihood profiles {#sec-likelihood-profile}

The likelihood profile over the mean total biomass for the diagnostic model showed conflict among the data sources. Most notable was the strong preference of the CPUE data and to a lesser degree the size data for lower biomass versus the tag data that preferred higher biomass (Figure @fig-diag-profile-data-sources). The CAAL data tend to preferred higher biomass than the CPUE and size data, but had a flat profile through most of the biomass range, and the region of the overall likelihood. The penalty terms also preferred lower biomass. The conflict between the CPUE and tagging indicates that tag data is the key influence on higher biomass scaling. This conflict is accounted for to an extent in the uncertainty ensemble through higher mixing period scenarios, the alternative approaches to reporting rate adjustments in the mixing period, alternative ($\tau$).

The likelihood profiles can be explored in the [interactive HTML viewer](https://pacificcommunity.github.io/ofp-sam-bet-2026-diagnostic/bet-2026-likelihood-profile-viewer.html).

Given the conflict with the tagging data and assumptions required for modeling this data we explored likelihood profiles on the three tagging programs (Figure @fig-diag-profile-data-tag-prog). This showed that the tropical focussed PTTP is the main program that is preferring a higher biomass scale. The RTTP is less influential but also tends towards higher biomass. The JPTP, which is in region 1 is in conflict with the two tropical programs. This is perhaps not surprising given these programmes are spatially separated, and represent very different regions of the bigeye stock in the WCPO. Of more interest is the profiles of the tag release groups (Figure @fig-diag-profile-data-tag-prog-grps. There are no standout release group profiles for any of the individual programmes, and only one PTTP and one RTTP release group prefers lower biomass.

### ASPM {#sec-aspm}

Not done yet

Overall, from these diagnostics, acknowledging the tag data conflict would need to be considered as uncertainty, we were comfortable that diagnostic was satisfactory for conducting the sensitivity analysis as the basis for the uncertainty ensemble.

Population dynamics estimates
-----------------------------

A summary of the diagnostic model population dynamic quantities, $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$, $SB$, recruitment and $F$, is provided in Figure @fig-diag-time-series

### Selectivity {#sec-selectivity}

A range of selectivity curves are estimated for the different fisheries in the model and can be largely classified by gear type. The age-specific selectivity patterns are shown in Figure @fig-select-age and length-specific selectivity patterns are shown in Figure @fig-select-length.

### Movement {#sec-movement}

The model estimated very low movement rates among model regions (Figure @fig-season-movement-coeff). There was virtually no movement from region 1 to any other regions and very minor movement from region 2, 3 and 4 into region 1. Region 3, 4 and 5 showed the most connection with other regions. Region 2 showed some movement to region 3.

### Natural mortality {#sec-natM}

The Lorenzen form of natural mortality for the diagnostic model (Figure @fig-natm-at-age) had the scale set by the fixed M at age 40 quarter of 0.078/quarter. The Lorenzen shape of the natural mortality at age depends on the growth curve estimated in MFCL, and features considerably higher levels of natural mortality at age for very young fish with quarterly M approaching 0.45 at 1 quarter age, and a lower asymptote for mortality of the oldest age classes reached the fixed value of 0.078/quarter at age 40 quarters.

### Maturity {#sec-maturity-at-age}

Maturity-at-age is derived from the fixed maturity-at-length (fixed at the same values used in the 2023 diagnostic model) and applying the estimated growth curve to this to get maturity-at-age for the 2026 diagnostic model. This maturity-at-age curve differs slightly from the 2026 diagnostic model (Figure @fig-maturity-ogive) due to the differences in growth curves in these two models.

### Growth {#sec-growth-param}

The diagnostic model growth curve in is shown Figure @fig-growth-curve, and had the following estimated parameters: L1 25.68 cm (SD 4.03), L2 156.43 cm (SD 14.32), K 0.0956

### Recruitment: diagnostic model {#sec-recruitment-diag}

Total annual recruitment fluctuated widely across the time period but was generally between about 30 to 120 million individuals Figure @fig-recruitment-annual. There was a period of lower estimated recruitment from the 1960s to the 1990s, after which the trend stabilised fluctuating from 40 to 120 million individuals per year. At the regional level there was high interannual variation and trends for some region. For example, region 1 shows a sharp decline from the 1950s until 1980 after which it stabilises, whereas region 2 and 3 increase from 1980 onwards, other regions have periods of higher and lower levels. Region 1 and region 3 tend to contribute the most recruitment Figure @fig-recruitment-regions.

The fit to the stock recruitment relationship for the 2026 diagnostic model is shown in Figure @fig-stock-rr.

### Spawning potential and depletion: diagnostic model {#sec-biomass-diag}

The 2026 diagnostic model estimates an initial steep decline in the overall spawning potential, from the late 1950s through until the mid 1980s, followed by a more stable period until the late 1990s, then a further decline until around 2010, after which it has remained fairly stable through to the final year, which shows a small drop (Figure @fig-diag-time-series). The pattern in the decline in spawning potential over time, is consistent with the CPUE indices Figure @fig-cpue-fit-1-5 and mirrors the catch history, that has reduced and stabilised since 2010 (Figure @fig-catch-hist-full).

The 2026 diagnostic model shows a decline in overall spawning potential depletion, $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ through to the mid 1960s when there is a more stable period, followed by decline through to about 2010, after which it levels off just below 0.2 Figure @fig-diag-time-series. As with spawning potential, the dynamic trend mirrors the catch history, with the more recent stability reflecting more stable average catches.

The relative levels of total biomass, spawning potential and recruitment among the model regions for the diagnostic model is shown in Figure @fig-timeseries-model-regions-stack.

### Fished (SB) versus unfished (SB$_{F=0}$) spawning potential: diagnostic model {#sec-fished-unfished-diag}

### Fishing mortality: diagnostic model {#sec-fish-mortality-diag}

Overall fishing mortality (F) increases since 1970s before stabilising with interannual fluctuations between approximately 0.3 to 0.6 per year since 2010 Figure @fig-diag-time-series.

Differences over time in the estimated adult and juvenile fishing mortality are shown in Figure @fig-juv-adult-F, with a gradual increase in overall adult fishing mortality up until around 2000, with relatively stable adult mortality since then. The uptick in the final year for adult mortality likely relates to the increase in catch attributed to the large fish handline fishery due to Indonesia's change in how they allocate catch between the small fish (part of other gears domestic fishery) and large fish handline, which requires an historical adjustment based on Indonesia's advice before the next bigeye assessment. Fishing mortality of juveniles starts to increase above that of adults from around 1980 with the expansion of the purse seine associated catch fisheries, and continues above adult mortality stabilising from 2010, with a recent peak in 2022-2023. The recent peak appears related to increased juvenile fishing mortality by the fisheries operating in regions 2 and 3, which along with region 4 are the highest contributors to both adult and juvenile fishing mortality Figure @fig-juv-adult-F.

Sensitivity analyses {#sec-sensitivity-results}
--------------------

The results of all sensitivity analysis can be explored in the [interactive HTML viewer](https://pacificcommunity.github.io/ofp-sam-bet-2026-sensitivity/bet-2026-sensitivity-interactive-viewer.html). All the sensitivity models achieved a suitable gradient and had positive definite Hessian status.

### Steepness {#sec-oneoff-steepness}

The sensitivity on steepness had some impacts on $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$, with more depleted stock when applying lower steepness values Figure @fig-sensitivity-steepness.

### Natural mortality {#sec-oneoff-natural-mortality}

The sensitivity on M at age 40 quarters had notable impacts $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$, with more depleted (pessimistic) stock status when applying the diagnostic value, and less depleted (more optimistic) status when applying both the higher and the lower values Figure @fig-sensitivity-natural-mortality. The more optimistic depletion status and notably higher spawning potential scale for the lowest value was unexpected and requires further consideration. The highest M value produced the highest recruitment and lowest fishing mortality mortality.

### CAAL data weighting {#sec-oneoff-caal-data-weighting}

The sensitivity on the CAAL data weighting had minor effects on the terminal $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$, and $SB$. The highest downweighting of 0.5 produced a more optimistic depletion status, higher recruitment, and also higher historic $SB$ (Figure @fig-sensitivity-CAAL).

### Effort creep on CPUE {#sec-oneoff-effort-creep}

The sensitivity on the level of effort creep had no impact on the terminal levels of $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$, $SB$, fishing mortality or recruitment. The higher effort creep scenario produced higher initial $SB$ and recruitment and steeper declining trends (Figure @fig-sensitivity-effort-creep).

### CPUE time period for regional scaling {#sec-oneoff-regional-scaling}

The sensitivity on the choice of the time period for the global CPUE to use in the regional scaling penalty was impactful on the $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$, $SB$, fishing mortality and recruitment. Applying the full time period of the CPUE series rather than the shorter early time period of maximum coverage used in the diagnostic case (i.e 1965-1969, as recommended in PAW), produced higher population scale ($SB$), lower F and higher recruitment, with a more optimistic depletion (Figure @fig-sensitivity-effort-creep).

### Tag mixing {#sec-oneoff-tag-mixing}

The sensitivity on the choice of the K-statistic for assigning release specific tag mixing periods was impactful on $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$, $SB$, recruitment and fishing mortality. The lower value of 0.1 which results in more conservative longer tag mixing periods produced higher $SB$ scale and a less depleted, more optimistic $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$, also higher recruitment and lower fishing mortality (Figure @fig-sensitivity-tag-mixing-periods-Kstatistic-cutoff).

### Reporting rates adjustment in the mixing periods {#sec-oneoff-rr-during-mixing-period}

The sensitivity on the choice of activating of deactivating tag reporting rate adjustments in the mixing period was not impactful on $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$, $SB$, recruitment and fishing mortality. This lack of impact was unexpected and may relate to the tau value of 2 downnweighting the tag data as did see impact of this in the stepwise model development when tau was set to 1 (Figure @fig-sensitivity-tag-mixing-periods-Kstatistic-cutoff).

### Tau overdispersion parameter {#sec-oneoff-tau}

The sensitivity on the choice of the overdispersion parameter ($\tau$) was impactful on $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$, $SB$, recruitment and fishing mortality when it was set below 1.4, settings above 1.4 were very similar. At lower than 1.4, $SB$ scale increased, $SB$/$SB_{F=0}$ increased to more optimistic levels, recruitment increased and fishing mortality decreased (Figure @fig-sensitivity-tag-overdispersion).
